search_paper_list.title: Diffusion Map Autoencoder
search_paper_list.summary:
In this work, we explore various modifications to diffusion maps (DMAP),
including their incorporation into a layered sequential neural network model
trained with gradient descent. The result is a sequential neural network that
inherits the interpretability of diffusion maps.

search_paper_list.title:
NaturalSpeech 3: Zero-Shot Speech Synthesis with Factorized Codec and
  Diffusion Models
search_paper_list.summary:
While recent large-scale text-to-speech (TTS) models have achieved
significant progress, they still fall short in speech quality, similarity, and
prosody. Considering speech intricately encompasses various attributes (e.g.,
content, prosody, timbre, and acoustic details) that pose significant
challenges for generation, a natural idea is to factorize speech into
individual subspaces representing different attributes and generate them
individually. Motivated by it, we propose NaturalSpeech 3, a TTS system with
novel factorized diffusion models to generate natural speech in a zero-shot
way. Specifically, 1) we design a neural codec with factorized vector
quantization (FVQ) to disentangle speech waveform into subspaces of content,
prosody, timbre, and acoustic details; 2) we propose a factorized diffusion
model to generate attributes in each subspace following its corresponding
prompt. With this factorization design, NaturalSpeech 3 can effectively and
efficiently model intricate speech with disentangled subspaces in a
divide-and-conquer way. Experiments show that NaturalSpeech 3 outperforms the
state-of-the-art TTS systems on quality, similarity, prosody, and
intelligibility, and achieves on-par quality with human recordings.
Furthermore, we achieve better performance by scaling to 1B parameters and 200K
hours of training data.

search_paper_list.title:
Active matter beyond mean-field: Ring-kinetic theory for self-propelled
  particles
search_paper_list.summary:
A ring-kinetic theory for Vicsek-style models of self-propelled agents is
derived from the exact N-particle evolution equation in phase space. The theory
goes beyond mean-field and does not rely on Boltzmann's approximation of
molecular chaos. It can handle pre-collisional correlations and cluster
formation which both seem important to understand the phase transition to
collective motion. We propose a diagrammatic technique to perform a small
density expansion of the collision operator and derive the first two equations
of the BBGKY-hierarchy. An algorithm is presented that numerically solves the
evolution equation for the two-particle correlations on a lattice. Agent-based
simulations are performed and informative quantities such as orientational and
density correlation functions are compared with those obtained by ring-kinetic
theory. Excellent quantitative agreement between simulations and theory is
found at not too small noises and mean free paths. This shows that there is
parameter ranges in Vicsek-like models where the correlated closure of the
BBGKY-hierarchy gives correct and nontrivial results. We calculate the
dependence of the orientational correlations on distance in the disordered
phase and find that it seems to be consistent with a power law with exponent
around -1.8, followed by an exponential decay. General limitations of the
kinetic theory and its numerical solution are discussed.

search_paper_list.title: Learning a Diffusion Model Policy from Rewards via Q-Score Matching
search_paper_list.summary:
Diffusion models have become a popular choice for representing actor policies
in behavior cloning and offline reinforcement learning. This is due to their
natural ability to optimize an expressive class of distributions over a
continuous space. However, previous works fail to exploit the score-based
structure of diffusion models, and instead utilize a simple behavior cloning
term to train the actor, limiting their ability in the actor-critic setting. In
this paper, we present a theoretical framework linking the structure of
diffusion model policies to a learned Q-function, by linking the structure
between the score of the policy to the action gradient of the Q-function. We
focus on off-policy reinforcement learning and propose a new policy update
method from this theory, which we denote Q-score matching. Notably, this
algorithm only needs to differentiate through the denoising model rather than
the entire diffusion model evaluation, and converged policies through Q-score
matching are implicitly multi-modal and explorative in continuous domains. We
conduct experiments in simulated environments to demonstrate the viability of
our proposed method and compare to popular baselines. Source code is available
from the project website: https://michaelpsenka.io/qsm.

search_paper_list.title:
Isometric Representation Learning for Disentangled Latent Space of
  Diffusion Models
search_paper_list.summary:
The latent space of diffusion model mostly still remains unexplored, despite
its great success and potential in the field of generative modeling. In fact,
the latent space of existing diffusion models are entangled, with a distorted
mapping from its latent space to image space. To tackle this problem, we
present Isometric Diffusion, equipping a diffusion model with a geometric
regularizer to guide the model to learn a geometrically sound latent space of
the training data manifold. This approach allows diffusion models to learn a
more disentangled latent space, which enables smoother interpolation, more
accurate inversion, and more precise control over attributes directly in the
latent space. Our extensive experiments consisting of image interpolations,
image inversions, and linear editing show the effectiveness of our method.

search_paper_list.title:
Improving Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems Using Optimal Posterior
  Covariance
search_paper_list.summary:
Recent diffusion models provide a promising zero-shot solution to noisy
linear inverse problems without retraining for specific inverse problems. In
this paper, we reveal that recent methods can be uniformly interpreted as
employing a Gaussian approximation with hand-crafted isotropic covariance for
the intractable denoising posterior to approximate the conditional posterior
mean. Inspired by this finding, we propose to improve recent methods by using
more principled covariance determined by maximum likelihood estimation. To
achieve posterior covariance optimization without retraining, we provide
general plug-and-play solutions based on two approaches specifically designed
for leveraging pre-trained models with and without reverse covariance. We
further propose a scalable method for learning posterior covariance prediction
based on representation with orthonormal basis. Experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly enhance reconstruction
performance without requiring hyperparameter tuning.

search_paper_list.title: Hyperbolic Geometric Latent Diffusion Model for Graph Generation
search_paper_list.summary:
Diffusion models have made significant contributions to computer vision,
sparking a growing interest in the community recently regarding the application
of them to graph generation. Existing discrete graph diffusion models exhibit
heightened computational complexity and diminished training efficiency. A
preferable and natural way is to directly diffuse the graph within the latent
space. However, due to the non-Euclidean structure of graphs is not isotropic
in the latent space, the existing latent diffusion models effectively make it
difficult to capture and preserve the topological information of graphs. To
address the above challenges, we propose a novel geometrically latent diffusion
framework HypDiff. Specifically, we first establish a geometrically latent
space with interpretability measures based on hyperbolic geometry, to define
anisotropic latent diffusion processes for graphs. Then, we propose a
geometrically latent diffusion process that is constrained by both radial and
angular geometric properties, thereby ensuring the preservation of the original
topological properties in the generative graphs. Extensive experimental results
demonstrate the superior effectiveness of HypDiff for graph generation with
various topologies.

search_paper_list.title: Floating Anchor Diffusion Model for Multi-motif Scaffolding
search_paper_list.summary:
Motif scaffolding seeks to design scaffold structures for constructing
proteins with functions derived from the desired motif, which is crucial for
the design of vaccines and enzymes. Previous works approach the problem by
inpainting or conditional generation. Both of them can only scaffold motifs
with fixed positions, and the conditional generation cannot guarantee the
presence of motifs. However, prior knowledge of the relative motif positions in
a protein is not readily available, and constructing a protein with multiple
functions in one protein is more general and significant because of the
synergies between functions. We propose a Floating Anchor Diffusion (FADiff)
model. FADiff allows motifs to float rigidly and independently in the process
of diffusion, which guarantees the presence of motifs and automates the motif
position design. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of FADiff with high
success rates and designable novel scaffolds. To the best of our knowledge,
FADiff is the first work to tackle the challenge of scaffolding multiple motifs
without relying on the expertise of relative motif positions in the protein.
Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/FADiff.

search_paper_list.title: FiT: Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion Model
search_paper_list.summary:
Nature is infinitely resolution-free. In the context of this reality,
existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face
challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain.
To overcome this limitation, we present the Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT),
a transformer architecture specifically designed for generating images with
unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios. Unlike traditional methods that
perceive images as static-resolution grids, FiT conceptualizes images as
sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. This perspective enables a flexible
training strategy that effortlessly adapts to diverse aspect ratios during both
training and inference phases, thus promoting resolution generalization and
eliminating biases induced by image cropping. Enhanced by a meticulously
adjusted network structure and the integration of training-free extrapolation
techniques, FiT exhibits remarkable flexibility in resolution extrapolation
generation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance
of FiT across a broad range of resolutions, showcasing its effectiveness both
within and beyond its training resolution distribution. Repository available at
https://github.com/whlzy/FiT.

search_paper_list.title:
As Simple as Fine-tuning: LLM Alignment via Bidirectional Negative
  Feedback Loss
search_paper_list.summary:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a more computationally
efficient alternative to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) with
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), eliminating the need for reward models and
online sampling. Despite these benefits, DPO and its variants remain sensitive
to hyper-parameters and prone to instability, particularly on mathematical
datasets. We argue that these issues arise from the unidirectional
likelihood-derivative negative feedback inherent in the log-likelihood loss
function. To address this, we propose a novel LLM alignment loss that
establishes a stable Bidirectional Negative Feedback (BNF) during optimization.
Our proposed BNF loss eliminates the need for pairwise contrastive losses and
does not require any extra tunable hyper-parameters or pairwise preference
data, streamlining the alignment pipeline to be as simple as supervised
fine-tuning. We conduct extensive experiments across two challenging QA
benchmarks and four reasoning benchmarks. The experimental results show that
BNF achieves comparable performance to the best methods on QA benchmarks, while
its performance decrease on the four reasoning benchmarks is significantly
lower compared to the best methods, thus striking a better balance between
value alignment and reasoning ability. In addition, we further validate the
performance of BNF on non-pairwise datasets, and conduct in-depth analysis of
log-likelihood and logit shifts across different preference optimization
methods.

Github Url: https://github.com/MaoXinn/BNF/.1 I NTRODUCTIONAlignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) plays a pivotal role in ensuring that these LLMsbehave in accordance with human values and expectations (Bai et al., 2022b). As LLMs becomeincreasingly integrated into various applications (Zhang et al., 2023; Roziere et al., 2023), ensuringproper alignment is crucial to mitigate risks such as biased or harmful outputs, while also enhanc-ing trustworthiness. One of the most prominent LLM alignment methods is Reinforcement Learn-ing from Human Feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022) with Proximal Policy Optimization (RLHF-PPO)(Schulman et al., 2017), which underpins the success of ChatGPT. However, despite its achieve-ments, RLHF-PPO faces notable limitations, particularly regarding the high computational costsassociated with reward modeling and online sampling (Casper et al., 2023). These challenges com-plicate its widespread adoption, especially in scenarios where computational resources are limited.In response to these limitations, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) and itsderivative methods (Ethayarajh et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023) aim to simplify the overall alignmentpipeline by eliminating the need for reward and value models, as well as online sampling. Despiteachieving impressive performance on QA and Chatbot tasks (Meng et al., 2024), DPO-series meth-ods remain highly sensitive to hyper-parameters and often exhibit instability (Xu et al., 2024b). Thisinstability is particularly pronounced when applied to mathematical datasets, leading to potentialtraining collapse (Pal et al., 2024). Recently, several efforts (Xu et al., 2024a; Pal et al., 2024) havebeen made to address this issue. They attribute the collapse to an erroneous decrease in the like-lihood of the preferred samples and propose using Negative Log Likelihood (NLL) regularizationto stabilize the training process. As shown in Figure 1, when applying theNLL loss to increase the likelihood πθ(yw|x) = ezywP|V|k=1 ezkof apreferred output yw, the partial derivative   ∂LNLL∂zyw    with respectto the unnormalized logit zyw will gradually decrease, whichlimits the rate of future increases in zyw and πθ(yw|x), pre-venting the model from over-fitting. However, when the sameloss is used to decrease the likelihood of a dispreferred outputyl, this negative feedback turns into a positive one. Asπθ(yl|x)decreases,   ∂−LNLL∂zyl    continues to rise, which further acceler-ates subsequent decreases in zyl and πθ(yl|x), ultimately re-sulting in model collapse. To mitigate this issue, DPO-seriesmethods introduce pairwise contrastive losses to constrain the likelihood ofyl from deviating exces-sively from that of the preferred sampleyw. However, this constraint is sensitive to hyper-parametersand lacks stability, resulting in the failure of DPO on mathematical datasets in practice.Based on the above findings, we propose a novel alignment loss, Bidirectional Negative Feedback(BNF) loss. As shown in Figure 1, when optimizing with BNF loss, the partial derivative    ∂L∂zy   reaches its maximum only when πθ(y|x) =πref(y|x) (i.e., the initial state). Whether the likelihoodπθ(y|x) increases or decreases,    ∂L∂zy    decreases linearly in both directions, thus establishing a bidi-rectional negative feedback. Since this bidirectional negative feedback fundamentally addresses theissue of excessive decreases in the likelihood of dispreferred samples, BNF eliminates the need forpairwise contrastive losses, further streamlining the alignment pipeline to be as simple as supervisedfine-tuning. In summary, BNF loss offers the following advantages:• Less alignment tax: Recent studies (Ouyang et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023) have shown that usingpreference optimization methods to align LLMs with human values often harms their reasoningability, referred to as the alignment tax. With the bidirectional negative feedback, our proposedBNF can naturally prevent the model from over-fitting to preference data, striking a better balancebetween human values and reasoning ability while minimizing the alignment tax.• Fewer tunable hyper-parameters: Since the need for pairwise contrastive losses is eliminated,our proposed BNF loss does not involve any extra tunable hyper-parameters such as scaling factorβ in DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), margin γ in SimPO (Meng et al., 2024) or NLL regularizationweight λ in SLiC (Zhao et al., 2023), which significantly reduces the cost of grid searches.• Less pairwise data: In addition to fewer tunable hyper-parameters, the removal of pairwise con-trastive losses means that BNF no longer relies on pairwise preference data. Then, we explain how DPO-series methods mitigate this excessive decrease by employinga pairwise contrastive loss, and why this approach is ineffective for mathematical datasets.2.1 L IMITATION OF LOG-LIKELIHOOD LOSSIn the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage, we typically only use the NLL loss to maximize thelikelihood of each sample from the dataset without worrying about collapse. In the alignment stage,a naive approach would be to try the following log-likelihood loss for preference optimization:LNLL+PLL = E(x,yw,yl)∼D[−log πθ(yw|x) + logπθ(yl|x)] (1)This naive loss tries to increase the likelihood of the preferred sampleyw with NLL and decrease thelikelihood of the dispreferred sample yl with Positive Log Likelihood (PLL). However, LLMs willquickly collapse when optimized with the above loss (Rafailov et al., 2023). As mentioned in Section1, the underlying reason is the unidirectional likelihood-derivative negative feedback inherent in thelog-likelihood loss. Let’s consider a simple case where the response y consists of only a singletoken. When we apply the NLL loss to increase the likelihood πθ(yw|x) of the preferred yw:LNLL = E(x,yw)∼D[−log πθ(yw|x)] =E(x,yw)∼D"−log ezywP|V|k=1 ezk#(2)where |V| is the vocabulary size. In this case, the likeli-hood πθ(yw|x) and the partial derivative   ∂LNLL∂zyw    actually establish a stable negative feedback. Asπθ(yw|x) increases, |∂LNLL∂zyw| gradually decreases, which limits the rate of future increases inzyw andπθ(yw|x), thereby preventing the model from over-fitting.However, this negative feedback is unidirectional. Since our proposed BNF loss does not have any extra tunable hyper-parameters, we only perform grid searches on batch size {64, 128, 256} and learning rate {5e-7,6e-7, 8e-7, 1e-6}. After grid search, we adopt a unified batch size of 128 and select learning rates of5e-7 for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, 6e-7 for Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and 8e-7 for Gemma-2-9b-it.Baselines. (5) SimPO (Meng et al., 2024) is a simpler andeffective preference optimization method without using a reference model. Inaddition, we provide some response comparisons in Appendix D for reference.5.1 M AIN EXPERIMENT ANALYSISPreference optimization is essential for QA.From Table 4, we observe that all three base modelsrank the lowest on two QA benchmarks, Wild-Bench and Arena-Hard, while all preference opti-mization methods achieve significant performance improvements. More specifically, DPO, SimPO,and our proposed BNF demonstrate superior performance compared to other methods, consistentlysecuring the top three positions across all QA metrics. DPO performs best on Meta-Llama-3, SimPOworks best on Mistral-7B, and our proposed BNF exhibits outstanding performance on Gemma-2.These experimental results indicate that preference optimization is essential for improving modelperformance on QA tasks and demonstrate that our proposed BNF can deliver performance compa-rable to, or even superior to, the strongest preference optimization baselines.BNF pays the lowest alignment tax.When our attention shifts to reasoning benchmarks, we findthat the methods excelling in QA benchmarks often perform poorly in reasoning benchmarks, whichis also referred to as alignment tax (Ouyang et al., 2022). For instance, SimPO, which performswell on QA, experiences a significant drop in performance on reasoning, with a more than 10%performance decrease on GSM8K, ranking nearly at the bottom. In contrast, KTO, which excels inreasoning benchmarks, performs poorly on QA benchmarks, only slightly better than base models.Some studies (Lin et al., 2023) suggest that alignment tax occurs due to over-fitting to preferencedata, leading to a decline in reasoning ability. With the bidirectional negative feedback, our proposedBNF can automatically constrain the model from over-fitting to preference datasets, thus preservingthe reasoning ability. The typicalRLHF pipeline consists of three stages: Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT), reward model training, andpolicy optimization. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) is commonly usedin the policy optimization stage to align the model with human feedback. RLHF has been appliedacross various domains, including mitigating toxicity (Chaudhari et al., 2024), enhancing reasoningabilities (Wang et al., 2024b), and improving the helpfulness of language models (Bai et al., 2022a).However, RLHF often requires complex hyper-parameter tuning and can be unstable, primarily dueto the sensitivity of the reward model (Casper et al., 2023). In contrast, Direct Preference Optimiza-tion (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) simplifies this process by removing the need for an explicit rewardmodel, directly optimizing for preferences. This makes DPO a more resource-efficient alternativeto RLHF. While DPO addresses some of RLHF’s complexities, further improvements and variantshave been proposed to overcome specific challenges in preference optimization.6.2 C HALLENGES OF DIRECT PREFERENCE OPTIMIZATIONAlthough DPO-series methods have demonstrated impressive performance on QA and Chatbot tasks(Meng et al., 2024), they remain highly sensitive to hyper-parameters and often exhibit instability(Xu et al., 2024b). This instability is especially evident when applied to mathematical datasets,potentially leading to training collapse (Pal et al., 2024). Recent studies (Zhao et al., 2023; Xuet al., 2024a) propose using Negative Log Likelihood (NLL) regularization to stabilize training.While these approaches successfully prevent collapse on mathematical datasets, they perform poorlyon several popular Chat and QA benchmarks (Meng et al., 2024) and introduce additional hyper-parameters. Another significant challenge in preference optimization is controlling the output length,as models trained with DPO tend to produce verbose responses that may reduce the quality of results(Xu et al., 2024b). To address this, several DPO variants have been developed. For instance, SimPO(Meng et al., 2024) applies a length-normalized reward to prevent the generation of excessively longoutputs. RDPO (Park et al., 2024) adds a regularization term to reduce length exploitation.7 C ONCLUSION , LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORKConclusion. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM alignment loss with Bidirectional NegativeFeedback (BNF), addressing the instability and hyper-parameter sensitivity found in DPO and itsvariants. Unlike DPO-series methods, BNF eliminates the need for pairwise contrastive lossesand preference data, streamlining the alignment pipeline to be as simple as supervised fine-tuning.Our experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that BNF achieves strong performance on QAbenchmarks, while preserving the reasoning ability of LLMs and paying the lowest alignment tax.Limitations and Future work. Despite our efforts to improve this work, due to constraints incomputational resources and budgets, there are still the following limitations:• Model Scale. All the experiments in this paper are based on LLMs of 7B-9B scales, and we areunsure whether our proposed method can be stably scaled to larger LLMs of 30B or more.• Combination with DPO-series methods.Our proposed BNF loss is not necessarily opposedto DPO-series methods; in fact, the two approaches can be complementary, and introducing apairwise contrastive function may further improve the performance and stability of BNF.• Non-pairwise Dataset. The non-pairwise dataset used in this paper is derived from a regularpreference dataset with random masking, which is merely a simulation and may not fully reflectreal-world applications.preference dataset with random masking, which is merely a simulation and may not fully reflectreal-world applications.These limitations will also serve as the starting point for our future work. candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Purify++: Improving Diffusion-Purification with Advanced Diffusion
  Models and Control of Randomness
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Adversarial attacks can mislead neural network classifiers. The defense
against adversarial attacks is important for AI safety. Adversarial
purification is a family of approaches that defend adversarial attacks with
suitable pre-processing. Diffusion models have been shown to be effective for
adversarial purification. Despite their success, many aspects of diffusion
purification still remain unexplored. In this paper, we investigate and improve
upon three limiting designs of diffusion purification: the use of an improved
diffusion model, advanced numerical simulation techniques, and optimal control
of randomness. Based on our findings, we propose Purify++, a new diffusion
purification algorithm that is now the state-of-the-art purification method
against several adversarial attacks. Our work presents a systematic exploration
of the limits of diffusion purification methods.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Purify++, a novel diffusion purification algorithm that enhances adversarial robustness by improving upon three key aspects of diffusion purification: the diffusion model itself, numerical simulation techniques, and control of randomness. The research demonstrates state-of-the-art purification performance against several adversarial attacks.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: Purify++ leverages an improved diffusion model (EDM, a generalization of VE diffusion), advanced sampling techniques (Heun's method for efficient simulation of purification SDE), and optimal control of randomness (a linear combination of ODE and Langevin dynamics) to pre-process input data and mitigate adversarial perturbations.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets using various classifiers (LeNet, Residual Networks, Wide ResNet). Performance is measured using standard and robust accuracy against black-box (Square Attack, SPSA), gray-box (PGD), and adaptive (BPDA+EOT) attacks. The experiments also include ablation studies to assess the contribution of each component of Purify++.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The evaluation of Purify++ against the BPDA+EOT attack is performed on a subset of the CIFAR10 test set due to the high computational cost. Also, the paper focuses primarily on ℓp-norm bounded threat models.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: The paper suggests further developments in diffusion-based purification methods, implying potential research into new architectures, sampling techniques, and methods for controlling randomness. Also exploring the application of Purify++ to other data modalities and tasks could be a future research direction.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Consistent Diffusion Meets Tweedie: Training Exact Ambient Diffusion
  Models with Noisy Data
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Ambient diffusion is a recently proposed framework for training diffusion
models using corrupted data. Both Ambient Diffusion and alternative SURE-based
approaches for learning diffusion models from corrupted data resort to
approximations which deteriorate performance. We present the first framework
for training diffusion models that provably sample from the uncorrupted
distribution given only noisy training data, solving an open problem in this
space. Our key technical contribution is a method that uses a double
application of Tweedie's formula and a consistency loss function that allows us
to extend sampling at noise levels below the observed data noise. We also
provide further evidence that diffusion models memorize from their training
sets by identifying extremely corrupted images that are almost perfectly
reconstructed, raising copyright and privacy concerns. Our method for training
using corrupted samples can be used to mitigate this problem. We demonstrate
this by fine-tuning Stable Diffusion XL to generate samples from a distribution
using only noisy samples. Our framework reduces the amount of memorization of
the fine-tuning dataset, while maintaining competitive performance.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
A Diffusion Model Framework for Unsupervised Neural Combinatorial
  Optimization
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Learning to sample from intractable distributions over discrete sets without
relying on corresponding training data is a central problem in a wide range of
fields, including Combinatorial Optimization. Currently, popular deep
learning-based approaches rely primarily on generative models that yield exact
sample likelihoods. This work introduces a method that lifts this restriction
and opens the possibility to employ highly expressive latent variable models
like diffusion models. Our approach is conceptually based on a loss that upper
bounds the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence and evades the requirement of
exact sample likelihoods. We experimentally validate our approach in data-free
Combinatorial Optimization and demonstrate that our method achieves a new
state-of-the-art on a wide range of benchmark problems.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces DiffUCO, a diffusion model framework for unsupervised neural combinatorial optimization (NCO). It addresses the challenge of data-free approximation of discrete distributions in combinatorial optimization by using an upper bound on the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence as a loss function, enabling the application of latent variable models like diffusion models. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on a range of benchmark problems.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: DiffUCO employs a diffusion model that iteratively transforms a target distribution into a stationary distribution through a forward diffusion process. The reverse process is modeled to map samples from the stationary distribution back to the target distribution. The model is trained by minimizing a Joint Variational Upper Bound on the reverse KL divergence. The paper also introduces a more efficient version of Conditional Expectation sampling strategy using Subgraph Tokenization.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on five combinatorial optimization problems: Maximum Independent Set (MIS), Maximum Clique (MaxCl), Minimum Dominating Set (MDS), Maximum Cut (MaxCut), and Minimum Vertex Cover (MVC). candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions include improving the memory and time efficiency of DiffUCO, potentially by reducing the computational graph during backpropagation. candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Sequential Neural Score Estimation: Likelihood-Free Inference with
  Conditional Score Based Diffusion Models
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
We introduce Sequential Neural Posterior Score Estimation (SNPSE), a
score-based method for Bayesian inference in simulator-based models. Our
method, inspired by the remarkable success of score-based methods in generative
modelling, leverages conditional score-based diffusion models to generate
samples from the posterior distribution of interest. The model is trained using
an objective function which directly estimates the score of the posterior. We
embed the model into a sequential training procedure, which guides simulations
using the current approximation of the posterior at the observation of
interest, thereby reducing the simulation cost. We also introduce several
alternative sequential approaches, and discuss their relative merits. We then
validate our method, as well as its amortised, non-sequential, variant on
several numerical examples, demonstrating comparable or superior performance to
existing state-of-the-art methods such as Sequential Neural Posterior
Estimation (SNPE).
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Sequential Neural Posterior Score Estimation (SNPSE), a novel score-based method for Bayesian inference in simulator-based models. It leverages conditional score-based diffusion models to sample from the posterior distribution, trained using an objective function that estimates the posterior score directly. The method includes a sequential training procedure to reduce simulation costs and is validated against state-of-the-art methods.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The methodology utilizes conditional score-based diffusion models, where noise is gradually added to the target distribution using a diffusion process, resulting in a tractable reference distribution (e.g., Gaussian). Score matching techniques are used to approximate the score of the posterior, and a neural network is trained to estimate this score. The reverse-time diffusion process is then simulated to generate samples from the posterior.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is validated on several numerical examples and benchmark SBI problems, including the 'Two Moons' experiment, SLCP, Lotka-Volterra, and a real-world neuroscience problem involving a simulator model of the pyloric network in crabs. Performance is evaluated using the classification-based two-sample test (C2ST) score and by comparing posterior predictive samples with observed data.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The main limitation is the computational cost associated with computing the highest probability region (HPR) of the approximate posterior to define the proposal, which involves computationally expensive density evaluation using continuous normalizing flows (CNFs).
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions include developing sequential variants of Flow Matching Posterior Estimation (FMPE), exploring more specialized neural network architectures for SBI problems, and investigating alternative parameterizations of the score network to reduce computational cost.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Purify++: Improving Diffusion-Purification with Advanced Diffusion
  Models and Control of Randomness
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Adversarial attacks can mislead neural network classifiers. The defense
against adversarial attacks is important for AI safety. Adversarial
purification is a family of approaches that defend adversarial attacks with
suitable pre-processing. Diffusion models have been shown to be effective for
adversarial purification. Despite their success, many aspects of diffusion
purification still remain unexplored. In this paper, we investigate and improve
upon three limiting designs of diffusion purification: the use of an improved
diffusion model, advanced numerical simulation techniques, and optimal control
of randomness. Based on our findings, we propose Purify++, a new diffusion
purification algorithm that is now the state-of-the-art purification method
against several adversarial attacks. Our work presents a systematic exploration
of the limits of diffusion purification methods.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Purify++, a novel diffusion purification algorithm that enhances adversarial robustness by improving upon three key aspects of diffusion purification: the diffusion model itself, numerical simulation techniques, and control of randomness. The research demonstrates state-of-the-art purification performance against several adversarial attacks.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: Purify++ leverages an improved diffusion model (EDM, a generalization of VE diffusion), advanced sampling techniques (Heun's method for efficient simulation of purification SDE), and optimal control of randomness (a linear combination of ODE and Langevin dynamics) to pre-process input data and mitigate adversarial perturbations.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets using various classifiers (LeNet, Residual Networks, Wide ResNet). Performance is measured using standard and robust accuracy against black-box (Square Attack, SPSA), gray-box (PGD), and adaptive (BPDA+EOT) attacks. The experiments also include ablation studies to assess the contribution of each component of Purify++.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The evaluation of Purify++ against the BPDA+EOT attack is performed on a subset of the CIFAR10 test set due to the high computational cost. Also, the paper focuses primarily on ℓp-norm bounded threat models.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: The paper suggests further developments in diffusion-based purification methods, implying potential research into new architectures, sampling techniques, and methods for controlling randomness. Also exploring the application of Purify++ to other data modalities and tasks could be a future research direction.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Isometric Representation Learning for Disentangled Latent Space of
  Diffusion Models
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
The latent space of diffusion model mostly still remains unexplored, despite
its great success and potential in the field of generative modeling. In fact,
the latent space of existing diffusion models are entangled, with a distorted
mapping from its latent space to image space. To tackle this problem, we
present Isometric Diffusion, equipping a diffusion model with a geometric
regularizer to guide the model to learn a geometrically sound latent space of
the training data manifold. This approach allows diffusion models to learn a
more disentangled latent space, which enables smoother interpolation, more
accurate inversion, and more precise control over attributes directly in the
latent space. Our extensive experiments consisting of image interpolations,
image inversions, and linear editing show the effectiveness of our method.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Isometric Diffusion, a diffusion model equipped with a geometric regularizer to encourage the learning of a disentangled latent space. This leads to smoother interpolation, more accurate inversion, and more precise control over attributes directly in the latent space, addressing the problem of entangled latent spaces in existing diffusion models.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach involves equipping a diffusion model with an isometric representation learning framework. It introduces a novel loss function to encourage isometry between the latent space and the image space, guiding the model to learn a geometrically sound latent space that better reflects the data manifold. It uses stereographic coordinates to represent the latent space as a hypersphere manifold.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Church, and LSUN-Bedrooms datasets. Image quality is assessed using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). Disentanglement is measured using Perceptual Path Length (PPL) and Linear Separability (LS). A new metric, mean Relative Trajectory Length (mRTL), is introduced to measure the extent to which a trajectory in latent space is mapped to a geodesic in the semantic space. Mean Condition Number (MCN) and Variance of Riemannian metric (VoR) are also used.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: Applying the isometric regularizer introduces a trade-off between FID and disentanglement metrics. While disentanglement improves, FID scores may slightly worsen. Also, the complexity of H increases as the complexity of the training dataset increases.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions include applying the method to conditional generation tasks, such as text-to-image models, and exploring ways to minimize the trade-off between FID and disentanglement. Exploring the scalability of the method with large-scale training data and latent diffusion models is also suggested.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Improving Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems Using Optimal Posterior
  Covariance
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Recent diffusion models provide a promising zero-shot solution to noisy
linear inverse problems without retraining for specific inverse problems. In
this paper, we reveal that recent methods can be uniformly interpreted as
employing a Gaussian approximation with hand-crafted isotropic covariance for
the intractable denoising posterior to approximate the conditional posterior
mean. Inspired by this finding, we propose to improve recent methods by using
more principled covariance determined by maximum likelihood estimation. To
achieve posterior covariance optimization without retraining, we provide
general plug-and-play solutions based on two approaches specifically designed
for leveraging pre-trained models with and without reverse covariance. We
further propose a scalable method for learning posterior covariance prediction
based on representation with orthonormal basis. Experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly enhance reconstruction
performance without requiring hyperparameter tuning.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper addresses the problem of solving noisy linear inverse problems using diffusion models. It reveals that recent zero-shot diffusion-based methods can be uniformly interpreted as employing a Gaussian approximation with an isotropic covariance for the intractable denoising posterior. The main contribution is a generalized method to improve existing methods by optimizing the posterior covariance based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) without retraining. The paper proposes plug-and-play solutions for posterior covariance optimization and a scalable method for learning posterior covariance prediction based on orthonormal basis representation.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The methodology involves approximating the conditional posterior mean E[x0|xt, y] by optimizing the posterior covariance of the Gaussian approximation to the denoising posterior pt(x0|xt). Two plug-and-play methods are proposed: one leveraging reverse covariance prediction (if available) and another using Monte Carlo estimation (if reverse covariance is unavailable). For scalable covariance prediction, the paper proposes learning the variance in the transform space (e.g., using Discrete Wavelet Transform).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on FFHQ 256x256 and ImageNet 256x256 datasets. The proposed methods were evaluated on inpainting, deblurring (Gaussian and motion), and super-resolution tasks. Performance was measured using Structure Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), and Frechet Inception Distance (FID).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper acknowledges that the diagonal constraint on the covariance matrix limits the ability of the proposed method to perfectly match the optimum, even with a perfectly trained model.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring better principles for designing the covariance, leveraging nonlinear transformations for better correlation reduction, and investigating efficient approximations for Tweedie's approach.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: Hyperbolic Geometric Latent Diffusion Model for Graph Generation
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Diffusion models have made significant contributions to computer vision,
sparking a growing interest in the community recently regarding the application
of them to graph generation. Existing discrete graph diffusion models exhibit
heightened computational complexity and diminished training efficiency. A
preferable and natural way is to directly diffuse the graph within the latent
space. However, due to the non-Euclidean structure of graphs is not isotropic
in the latent space, the existing latent diffusion models effectively make it
difficult to capture and preserve the topological information of graphs. To
address the above challenges, we propose a novel geometrically latent diffusion
framework HypDiff. Specifically, we first establish a geometrically latent
space with interpretability measures based on hyperbolic geometry, to define
anisotropic latent diffusion processes for graphs. Then, we propose a
geometrically latent diffusion process that is constrained by both radial and
angular geometric properties, thereby ensuring the preservation of the original
topological properties in the generative graphs. Extensive experimental results
demonstrate the superior effectiveness of HypDiff for graph generation with
various topologies.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces HypDiff, a novel hyperbolic geometric latent diffusion model for graph generation, addressing the limitations of existing discrete graph diffusion models and the challenges of capturing and preserving topological information in latent space due to the anisotropy of non-Euclidean graph structures. The key contributions include studying the anisotropy of non-Euclidean structures for graph latent diffusion models from a geometric perspective, proposing a geometrically latent diffusion process based on radial and angular geometric constraints in hyperbolic space, and addressing the additivity of continuous Gaussian distributions and the issue of anisotropic noise addition in hyperbolic space.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The methodology involves establishing a geometrically latent space with interpretability measures based on hyperbolic geometry and defining anisotropic latent diffusion processes for graphs. It includes a hyperbolic geometric autoencoder (HGCN) to embed graphs into hyperbolic space, a geometrically latent diffusion process constrained by radial and angular geometric properties, and an approximate diffusion process based on radial measures to address the additivity issue of continuous Gaussian distribution in hyperbolic space. Angular constraints are utilized to preserve more structural prior, guiding the diffusion model to finer details of the graph structure. A denoising network based on UNET is used for training to predict the original node embeddings.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The model was evaluated on synthetic datasets (SBM, BA, Community, Ego, BA-G, Grid) and real-world datasets (Cora, Citeseer, Polblogs, MUTAG, IMDB-B, PROTEINS, COLLAB) for node classification and graph generation tasks. Performance was measured using F1 scores for node classification and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) scores (Degree, Cluster, Spectre) and F1 scores (precision-recall and density-coverage) for graph generation. Baselines included Euclidean graph representation methods (VGAE, ANE, GraphGAN), hyperbolic graph representation learning methods (P-V AE, Hype-ANE), deep graph generative models (GraphRNN), and graph diffusion generative models (GDSS, DiGress, GraphGDP, EDGE).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper acknowledges the challenges of additivity of continuous Gaussian distributions in hyperbolic latent space and proposes an approximate diffusion process based on radial measures to address it. The approximation may introduce some level of information loss or distortion. Also, the method's effectiveness might be sensitive to the choice of hyperbolic clustering parameter k and the radial popularity coefficient δ, requiring careful tuning based on the specific graph structure. The complexity analysis mentions a time complexity dependent on neural network operations, suggesting potential limitations with extremely large graphs depending on the specific implementation and hardware.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions could explore more sophisticated methods for handling the additivity issue of Gaussian distributions in hyperbolic space, potentially through alternative diffusion processes or geometric approximations. Further investigation into adaptive selection of the hyperbolic clustering parameter k and the radial popularity coefficient δ based on graph characteristics could improve performance. Additionally, exploring the application of HypDiff to dynamic graphs or graphs with node/edge features could broaden its applicability. The paper also suggests exploring improved sampling methods and recovery operators for the denoising process.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: FiT: Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion Model
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Nature is infinitely resolution-free. In the context of this reality,
existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face
challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain.
To overcome this limitation, we present the Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT),
a transformer architecture specifically designed for generating images with
unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios. Unlike traditional methods that
perceive images as static-resolution grids, FiT conceptualizes images as
sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. This perspective enables a flexible
training strategy that effortlessly adapts to diverse aspect ratios during both
training and inference phases, thus promoting resolution generalization and
eliminating biases induced by image cropping. Enhanced by a meticulously
adjusted network structure and the integration of training-free extrapolation
techniques, FiT exhibits remarkable flexibility in resolution extrapolation
generation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance
of FiT across a broad range of resolutions, showcasing its effectiveness both
within and beyond its training resolution distribution. Repository available at
https://github.com/whlzy/FiT.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces FiT (Flexible Vision Transformer), a novel transformer architecture for diffusion models that can generate images with unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios. Key contributions include a flexible training pipeline that eliminates cropping, a unique transformer architecture for dynamic token length modeling using 2D RoPE, and a training-free resolution extrapolation method (VisionNTK and VisionYaRN) for arbitrary resolution generation.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: FiT models images as sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. It employs a flexible training pipeline that adaptively resizes high-resolution images to fit within a maximum token limit, preserving the original aspect ratio. The architecture incorporates 2D Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), Swish-Gated Linear Unit (SwiGLU), and Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA). Training-free resolution extrapolation techniques, VisionNTK and VisionYaRN, are tailored for 2D RoPE to enhance performance across various resolutions and aspect ratios.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The FiT model was trained on the ImageNet dataset with a maximum token length of 256. The model's performance was evaluated using metrics such as Fre’chet Inception Distance (FID), sFID, Inception Score (IS), Precision, and Recall. candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
As Simple as Fine-tuning: LLM Alignment via Bidirectional Negative
  Feedback Loss
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a more computationally
efficient alternative to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) with
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), eliminating the need for reward models and
online sampling. Despite these benefits, DPO and its variants remain sensitive
to hyper-parameters and prone to instability, particularly on mathematical
datasets. We argue that these issues arise from the unidirectional
likelihood-derivative negative feedback inherent in the log-likelihood loss
function. To address this, we propose a novel LLM alignment loss that
establishes a stable Bidirectional Negative Feedback (BNF) during optimization.
Our proposed BNF loss eliminates the need for pairwise contrastive losses and
does not require any extra tunable hyper-parameters or pairwise preference
data, streamlining the alignment pipeline to be as simple as supervised
fine-tuning. We conduct extensive experiments across two challenging QA
benchmarks and four reasoning benchmarks. The experimental results show that
BNF achieves comparable performance to the best methods on QA benchmarks, while
its performance decrease on the four reasoning benchmarks is significantly
lower compared to the best methods, thus striking a better balance between
value alignment and reasoning ability. In addition, we further validate the
performance of BNF on non-pairwise datasets, and conduct in-depth analysis of
log-likelihood and logit shifts across different preference optimization
methods.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The proposed method introduces a Bidirectional Negative Feedback (BNF) loss. This loss function establishes a stable feedback mechanism during optimization by adjusting the target distribution of the cross-entropy loss. It dynamically adjusts the likelihood of preferred and dispreferred samples, ensuring that the model doesn't overfit to preference data and maintains reasoning ability.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The effectiveness of BNF is evaluated on two QA benchmarks (Arena-Hard and Wild-Bench) and four reasoning benchmarks (MMLU-redux, CRUX, GSM8K, and MATH-L5) using Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9b-it as base models. candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Isometric Representation Learning for Disentangled Latent Space of
  Diffusion Models
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
The latent space of diffusion model mostly still remains unexplored, despite
its great success and potential in the field of generative modeling. In fact,
the latent space of existing diffusion models are entangled, with a distorted
mapping from its latent space to image space. To tackle this problem, we
present Isometric Diffusion, equipping a diffusion model with a geometric
regularizer to guide the model to learn a geometrically sound latent space of
the training data manifold. This approach allows diffusion models to learn a
more disentangled latent space, which enables smoother interpolation, more
accurate inversion, and more precise control over attributes directly in the
latent space. Our extensive experiments consisting of image interpolations,
image inversions, and linear editing show the effectiveness of our method.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Isometric Diffusion, a diffusion model equipped with a geometric regularizer to encourage the learning of a disentangled latent space. This leads to smoother interpolation, more accurate inversion, and more precise control over attributes directly in the latent space, addressing the problem of entangled latent spaces in existing diffusion models.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach involves equipping a diffusion model with an isometric representation learning framework. It introduces a novel loss function to encourage isometry between the latent space and the image space, guiding the model to learn a geometrically sound latent space that better reflects the data manifold. It uses stereographic coordinates to represent the latent space as a hypersphere manifold.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Church, and LSUN-Bedrooms datasets. Image quality is assessed using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). Disentanglement is measured using Perceptual Path Length (PPL) and Linear Separability (LS). A new metric, mean Relative Trajectory Length (mRTL), is introduced to measure the extent to which a trajectory in latent space is mapped to a geodesic in the semantic space. Mean Condition Number (MCN) and Variance of Riemannian metric (VoR) are also used.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: Applying the isometric regularizer introduces a trade-off between FID and disentanglement metrics. While disentanglement improves, FID scores may slightly worsen. Also, the complexity of H increases as the complexity of the training dataset increases.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions include applying the method to conditional generation tasks, such as text-to-image models, and exploring ways to minimize the trade-off between FID and disentanglement. Exploring the scalability of the method with large-scale training data and latent diffusion models is also suggested.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Improving Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems Using Optimal Posterior
  Covariance
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Recent diffusion models provide a promising zero-shot solution to noisy
linear inverse problems without retraining for specific inverse problems. In
this paper, we reveal that recent methods can be uniformly interpreted as
employing a Gaussian approximation with hand-crafted isotropic covariance for
the intractable denoising posterior to approximate the conditional posterior
mean. Inspired by this finding, we propose to improve recent methods by using
more principled covariance determined by maximum likelihood estimation. To
achieve posterior covariance optimization without retraining, we provide
general plug-and-play solutions based on two approaches specifically designed
for leveraging pre-trained models with and without reverse covariance. We
further propose a scalable method for learning posterior covariance prediction
based on representation with orthonormal basis. Experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly enhance reconstruction
performance without requiring hyperparameter tuning.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper addresses the problem of solving noisy linear inverse problems using diffusion models. It reveals that recent zero-shot diffusion-based methods can be uniformly interpreted as employing a Gaussian approximation with an isotropic covariance for the intractable denoising posterior. The main contribution is a generalized method to improve existing methods by optimizing the posterior covariance based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) without retraining. The paper proposes plug-and-play solutions for posterior covariance optimization and a scalable method for learning posterior covariance prediction based on orthonormal basis representation.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The methodology involves approximating the conditional posterior mean E[x0|xt, y] by optimizing the posterior covariance of the Gaussian approximation to the denoising posterior pt(x0|xt). Two plug-and-play methods are proposed: one leveraging reverse covariance prediction (if available) and another using Monte Carlo estimation (if reverse covariance is unavailable). For scalable covariance prediction, the paper proposes learning the variance in the transform space (e.g., using Discrete Wavelet Transform).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on FFHQ 256x256 and ImageNet 256x256 datasets. The proposed methods were evaluated on inpainting, deblurring (Gaussian and motion), and super-resolution tasks. Performance was measured using Structure Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), and Frechet Inception Distance (FID).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper acknowledges that the diagonal constraint on the covariance matrix limits the ability of the proposed method to perfectly match the optimum, even with a perfectly trained model.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring better principles for designing the covariance, leveraging nonlinear transformations for better correlation reduction, and investigating efficient approximations for Tweedie's approach.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: Hyperbolic Geometric Latent Diffusion Model for Graph Generation
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Diffusion models have made significant contributions to computer vision,
sparking a growing interest in the community recently regarding the application
of them to graph generation. Existing discrete graph diffusion models exhibit
heightened computational complexity and diminished training efficiency. A
preferable and natural way is to directly diffuse the graph within the latent
space. However, due to the non-Euclidean structure of graphs is not isotropic
in the latent space, the existing latent diffusion models effectively make it
difficult to capture and preserve the topological information of graphs. To
address the above challenges, we propose a novel geometrically latent diffusion
framework HypDiff. Specifically, we first establish a geometrically latent
space with interpretability measures based on hyperbolic geometry, to define
anisotropic latent diffusion processes for graphs. Then, we propose a
geometrically latent diffusion process that is constrained by both radial and
angular geometric properties, thereby ensuring the preservation of the original
topological properties in the generative graphs. Extensive experimental results
demonstrate the superior effectiveness of HypDiff for graph generation with
various topologies.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces HypDiff, a novel hyperbolic geometric latent diffusion model for graph generation, addressing the limitations of existing discrete graph diffusion models and the challenges of capturing and preserving topological information in latent space due to the anisotropy of non-Euclidean graph structures. The key contributions include studying the anisotropy of non-Euclidean structures for graph latent diffusion models from a geometric perspective, proposing a geometrically latent diffusion process based on radial and angular geometric constraints in hyperbolic space, and addressing the additivity of continuous Gaussian distributions and the issue of anisotropic noise addition in hyperbolic space.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The methodology involves establishing a geometrically latent space with interpretability measures based on hyperbolic geometry and defining anisotropic latent diffusion processes for graphs. It includes a hyperbolic geometric autoencoder (HGCN) to embed graphs into hyperbolic space, a geometrically latent diffusion process constrained by radial and angular geometric properties, and an approximate diffusion process based on radial measures to address the additivity issue of continuous Gaussian distribution in hyperbolic space. Angular constraints are utilized to preserve more structural prior, guiding the diffusion model to finer details of the graph structure. A denoising network based on UNET is used for training to predict the original node embeddings.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The model was evaluated on synthetic datasets (SBM, BA, Community, Ego, BA-G, Grid) and real-world datasets (Cora, Citeseer, Polblogs, MUTAG, IMDB-B, PROTEINS, COLLAB) for node classification and graph generation tasks. Performance was measured using F1 scores for node classification and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) scores (Degree, Cluster, Spectre) and F1 scores (precision-recall and density-coverage) for graph generation. Baselines included Euclidean graph representation methods (VGAE, ANE, GraphGAN), hyperbolic graph representation learning methods (P-V AE, Hype-ANE), deep graph generative models (GraphRNN), and graph diffusion generative models (GDSS, DiGress, GraphGDP, EDGE).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper acknowledges the challenges of additivity of continuous Gaussian distributions in hyperbolic latent space and proposes an approximate diffusion process based on radial measures to address it. The approximation may introduce some level of information loss or distortion. Also, the method's effectiveness might be sensitive to the choice of hyperbolic clustering parameter k and the radial popularity coefficient δ, requiring careful tuning based on the specific graph structure. The complexity analysis mentions a time complexity dependent on neural network operations, suggesting potential limitations with extremely large graphs depending on the specific implementation and hardware.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future research directions could explore more sophisticated methods for handling the additivity issue of Gaussian distributions in hyperbolic space, potentially through alternative diffusion processes or geometric approximations. Further investigation into adaptive selection of the hyperbolic clustering parameter k and the radial popularity coefficient δ based on graph characteristics could improve performance. Additionally, exploring the application of HypDiff to dynamic graphs or graphs with node/edge features could broaden its applicability. The paper also suggests exploring improved sampling methods and recovery operators for the denoising process.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: FiT: Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion Model
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Nature is infinitely resolution-free. In the context of this reality,
existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face
challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain.
To overcome this limitation, we present the Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT),
a transformer architecture specifically designed for generating images with
unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios. Unlike traditional methods that
perceive images as static-resolution grids, FiT conceptualizes images as
sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. This perspective enables a flexible
training strategy that effortlessly adapts to diverse aspect ratios during both
training and inference phases, thus promoting resolution generalization and
eliminating biases induced by image cropping. Enhanced by a meticulously
adjusted network structure and the integration of training-free extrapolation
techniques, FiT exhibits remarkable flexibility in resolution extrapolation
generation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance
of FiT across a broad range of resolutions, showcasing its effectiveness both
within and beyond its training resolution distribution. Repository available at
https://github.com/whlzy/FiT.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: FiT models images as sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. It employs a flexible training pipeline that adaptively resizes high-resolution images to fit within a maximum token limit, preserving the original aspect ratio. The architecture incorporates 2D Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), Swish-Gated Linear Unit (SwiGLU), and Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA). Training-free resolution extrapolation techniques, VisionNTK and VisionYaRN, are tailored for 2D RoPE to enhance performance across various resolutions and aspect ratios.

The model's performance was evaluated using metrics such as Fre’chet Inception Distance (FID), sFID, Inception Score (IS), Precision, and Recall. Experiments were conducted across different aspect ratios (1:1, 1:2, 1:3) and resolutions, both within (256x256, 160x320, 128x384) and beyond (320x320, 224x448, 160x480) the training distribution. The FiT-XL/2 model was trained for 1.8 million steps.

The paper does not explore training FiT with higher resolutions (larger token length limitation) or resolution extrapolation methods that require additional training.

Below is the outcome of step 3—a completely new method that builds on Purify++ while incorporating ideas from optimal posterior covariance estimation to overcome some limitations of the base approach.

──────────────────────────────
Proposed Method: PurifyCov++: Covariance‐Optimized Diffusion Purification

Overview:
PurifyCov++ enhances the diffusion purification framework by adaptively controlling randomness not with fixed, hand‐crafted isotropic schemes but via an input‐dependent, learned covariance estimation. This method leverages optimal posterior covariance estimation (inspired by recent advances in inverse problems) and integrates it into the adversarial purification process. In doing so, it better aligns the denoising trajectory with the true data distribution—even under diverse or structured adversarial perturbations—while still benefiting from improvements already seen in Purify++ (advanced diffusion models and efficient numerical simulation).

Key Innovations:
1. Adaptive Covariance Estimation:  
 • Instead of using a fixed linear combination of ODE and Langevin components, PurifyCov++ employs a covariance prediction module (either trained via maximum likelihood on a mix of natural and adversarial examples or implemented in a plug‐and‐play fashion without extensive retraining).  
 • At each diffusion timestep, the module assesses the input’s local noise characteristics and predicts an optimal, possibly anisotropic, posterior covariance that better reflects the structure of adversarial perturbations.

2. Covariance-Driven Reverse Process:  
 • The reverse-time diffusion process is modified so that the magnitude and direction of the added randomness are explicitly scaled by the predicted covariance.  
 • This results in an adaptive purification whereby the randomness injected during denoising is tailored to maximally “cancel out” adversarial noise. The sampling step takes the form:  
  xₜ₋₁ = D(xₜ, t) + Σₜ⁽¹/²⁾ · ϵ,  
  where Σₜ (the covariance at time t) is predicted rather than predetermined, and D(·) denotes the deterministic component derived from advanced solvers (e.g., Heun’s method).

3. Enhanced Robustness Across Attack Modes:  
 • By dynamically estimating covariance, PurifyCov++ can adapt not only to ℓₚ-constrained perturbations targeted by Purify++ but also to more complex or structured adversarial noise whose statistical properties vary across the input space.  
 • As a result, the framework bridges the gap between fixed noise injection and the need for fine-grained uncertainty modeling in purification, leading to improvements in robust accuracy.

4. Efficient and Plug-and-Play Integration:  
 • The covariance prediction network is designed to be lightweight and can be integrated with pre-trained purification networks, allowing PurifyCov++ to benefit from state-of-the-art diffusion models without imposing a significant computational overhead.  
 • Alternatively, a Monte Carlo–based estimation can be used in scenarios where reverse covariance information is unavailable, endowing the method with flexibility.

Reasoning Behind PurifyCov++:
• Issue Addressed 1: Purify++ relies on fixed randomness control that may underperform against complex adversarial perturbations. Incorporating an adaptive, input-specific covariance estimation allows for a more precise “cancellation” of the adversarial noise.
• Issue Addressed 2: The base method’s focus on ℓₚ-norm bounded threat models can miss subtler forms of perturbation. By using an estimated covariance reflecting the actual noise structure, PurifyCov++ extends purification capabilities to a broader array of adversarial scenarios.
• Issue Addressed 3: Although Purify++ already utilizes advanced numerical simulations, the added adaptive covariance step changes the reverse process dynamics in a more principled way, potentially reducing the number of diffusion steps (and thus computational overhead) required to achieve effective purification.

Conclusion:
PurifyCov++ represents a truly new approach for adversarial purification. By marrying the advances from Purify++ (improved diffusion models, advanced numerical integration, and initial randomness control) with the principled posterior covariance estimation strategies from recent inverse-problem literature, this method provides an adaptive protection mechanism. The resulting purification process is more robust to diverse adversarial attacks while ideally reducing computational inefficiencies—a promising step forward in diffusion-based adversarial defense.

This outcome of step 3 describes a novel method that is more than a partial modification: it restructures the randomness management in diffusion purification from a fixed design into an adaptive, data-driven mechanism using optimal covariance prediction.

            adv_images = generate_fgsm_examples(classifier, images, labels, epsilon=0.03)
            
            # PurifyCov++:
            start = time.time()
            purified_cov = purify_diffusion(adv_images, steps, method='cov', covariance_net=covariance_net)
            elapsed_cov = time.time() - start
            total_time_cov += elapsed_cov
            
            # Purify++ (fixed):
            start = time.time()
            purified_fixed = purify_diffusion(adv_images, steps, method='fixed')
            elapsed_fixed = time.time() - start
            total_time_fixed += elapsed_fixed
            
            # Accuracy evaluation:
            preds_cov = classifier(purified_cov).argmax(dim=1)
            preds_fixed = classifier(purified_fixed).argmax(dim=1)
            acc_cov += (preds_cov == labels).sum().item()
            acc_fixed += (preds_fixed == labels).sum().item()
            
            # PSNR computation: assume 'images' are the clean images.
            purified_cov_cpu = purified_cov.detach().cpu().numpy()

        results['time_cov'].append(total_time_cov/len(test_loader))

    # Visualization of trade-offs:

In our implementation, we define dummy (but clearly marked) purification and covariance‐prediction routines so that you can later replace them with the actual reverse diffusion equations and learning strategies. We use PyTorch (with torchvision and torchattacks for adversarial examples), matplotlib for plotting (saved as PDF), and skimage for PSNR evaluation.
